This paper outlines a Rawlsian algorithm as an alternative to the Utilitarian solution. The algorithm will gather the vehicle’s estimation of probability of survival for each person in each action, then calculate which action a self-interested person would agree to if he or she were in an original bargaining position of fairness. I will employ Rawls’ assumption that the Maximin procedure is what self-interested agents would use from an original position, and then show how the Maximin procedure can be opera- tionalized to produce unique outputs over probabilities of survival. Keywords Autonomous vehicles · Ethics · Rawls · Trolley problem Introduction Trolley dilemmas occur when a runaway object is headed towards some group of people, and it’s possible to divert or block the train with an action that will result in the deaths of other people. Moral philosophers and psychologists are used to hearing this scenario criticized for being unrealistic and implausible. However, the newly emerging field of autonomous vehicles has recently provided a real-world trolley dilemma, and one that urgently needs to be solved * Derek Leben leben@pitt.edu before it happens, since the vehicles must be programmed with a decision-procedure prior to actually encountering the situation. The dilemma occurs when an autonomous vehicle is heading towards another vehicle or group of pedestrians, and does not have enough time to stop. In this situation, the vehicle can either swerve quickly, putting its own passengers at r isk of har m, or slow down1 as much as possible while continuing its dangerous course. Most people seem to assume that some version of Utili- tarianism provides the correct solution for this problem. In a recent survey of public responses, Bonnefon et al. (2016) found that laypeople overwhelmingly agree that swerv- ing is the correct decision in the situation described above (less so when it’s their own vehicle). Yet for those of us who believe that Utilitarianism is not the correct norma- tive guide to decision-making, it is important to outline an alternative. One alternative would be a decision-procedure based on the Principle of Double-Effect: the vehicle always continues its deadly path towards pedestrians, on the grounds that this is merely foreseen (and regrettable) harm, while swerving to intentionally harm passengers would be intentional harm. This is not the alternative that I wish to present here. Instead, I will describe a decision-procedure for this problem using the principles and methods advo- cated by Rawls (1971). Rawls’ moral theory has been incredibly influential within moral philosophy since its original publication, but as far as I’m aware, it has never been operationalized for machine decision-procedures. A ‘crash‐course’ in Contractarianism Rawls’ moral theory is usually categorized into the tra- dition of Contractarianism. The term ‘Contractarianism’ can refer to either a meta-ethical or a normative claim, and both will be adopted here. The meta-ethical claim is about the origin and purpose of moral rules; it states that moral principles are developed as solutions to the problem of social cooperation amongst self-interested organisms. The classic source for this view is Hobbes (1651), and has been endorsed in the twentieth century by Gauthier (1986), Binmore (2005), and Skyrms (2003). This view is described by Rawls in the opening pages of A Theory of Justice: D. Leben Then, although a society is a cooperative venture for mutual advantage, it is typically marked by a conflict as well as by an identity of interests. There is an identity of interests since social cooperation makes possible a better life for all than any would have if each were to live solely by his own efforts. There is a conflict of interests since persons are not indifferent as to how the greater benefits produced by their collaboration are distributed, for in order to pursue their ends they each prefer a larger to a lesser share. A set of principles is required for choosing among the various social arrangements which deter- mine this division of advantages and for underwrit- ing an agreement on the proper distributive shares. These principles are the principles of social justice: they provide a way of assigning rights and duties in the basic institutions of society and they define the appropriate distribution of the benefits and burdens of social cooperation (Rawls 1971, p. 4). The problem that Rawls describes here is prevalant in almost every part of human society. More food per per- son can be produced by agriculture than by hunting and gathering, but agriculture requires cooperation and stor- age which can be taken advantage of by thieves. Loaning money can be beneficial to both parties, but the lender always risks someone running off with her money. Two villages may gain strength by forming an alliance, but by letting their guards down, each runs the risk of its ally taking over. With the cooperators constantly put- ting themselves at such risk, one might expect that coop- eration is a rare occurrence in animal societies. How- ever, cooperation (both within and between species) is extremely common in both animal behavior and human societies. Thus, explaining how selfish organisms solve the problem of cooperation is a puzzle. Meta-ethical Con- tractarians suggest that moral principles and judgments have developed in order to overcome this challenge. Over the years, WhatsApp has become the most popular global messenger of all the world. These factors convinced us to use WhatsApp vocal messages to build our corpus. Participants were monitored during the online recording procedures via video call while they recorded their voices and performed the specific experimental speaking tasks given to them. Each participant had multiple attempts for each task, and at the end, one of their recordings was selected to be included in the corpus. Hans Annan, CFA, a food and beverage analyst, is reviewing Century Chocolate’s inventory policies as part of his evaluation of the company. Century Chocolate, based in Switzerland, manufactures chocolate products and purchases and resells other confectionery products to complement its chocolate line. Annan visited Century Chocolate’s manufacturing facility last year. He learned that cacao beans, imported from Brazil, represent the most significant raw material and that the work-in-progress inventory consists primarily of three items: roasted cacao beans, a thick paste produced from the beans (called chocolate liquor), and a sweetened mixture that needs to be “conched” to produce chocolate. On the tour, Annan learned that the conching process ranges from a few hours for lower-quality products to six days for the highest-quality chocolates. While there, Annan saw the facility’s climate-controlled area where manufactured finished products (cocoa and chocolate) and purchased finished goods are stored prior to shipment to customers. After touring the facility, Annan had a discussion with Century Chocolate’s CFO regarding the types of costs that were included in each inventory category. Annan has asked his assistant, Joanna Kern, to gather some preliminary information regarding Century Chocolate’s financial statements and inventories. He also asked Kern to calculate the inventory turnover ratios for Century Chocolate and another chocolate manufacturer for the most recent five years. There's what I'll call esoteric method, esoteric topics, and esoteric aesthetics. Esoteric method is a way of moving towards legible understanding of a thing through the intervening bog of informal considerations that can't yet be formulated with both clarity and generality. A lot of philosophy is in this mode, even as it rarely escapes it. Many technical problems are briefly in this mode before an appropriate formulation is found or legible desiderata can be stated. This is very inefficient and should be escaped whenever possible, which is not always. It takes at least a book to describe a practitioner's state of investigation with enough signal for another to continue the work, and progress is slow. Esoteric topics and esoteric aesthetics are in contrast the epistemically distortional phenomena that can be associated with practice of esoteric method and make it harder. An esoteric topic is one that's steeped in tradition of unclarity and anti-epistemic norms that maintain the equilibrium of unclarity. Many steps in the direction of escaping the bog and improving legibility get opposed by such traditions and norms, trivial inconvenience that makes continued use of the esoteric method impractical. It can be easier to make progress by escaping an esoteric topic and taking an outside perspective, while gaining enough access to it by hearing it out with charity. This is usually done without a need to also engage in practice of esoteric method within this outside perspective, so that only well-calibrated application of charity remains the unreliable step, with failure being failure to correctly understand the topic, rather than failure to sanely analyze it. But sometimes there is no legible way of analyzing it either, and so there are two difficulties at the same time, charity towards an esoteric topic in order to know what it's talking about, and sanity towards its investigation through esoteric method from an outside perspective, in order to both avoid the anti-epistemology that plagues the inside perspective of an esoteric topic, and make progress despite inability to say anything very legible for some time yet, the use of esoteric method. Esoteric aesthetics is an attitude that doesn't seek legibility, that enjoys unclarity. Fiction can be borne of esoteric aesthetics, and many practitioners of esoteric topics enjoy it, firming up the anti-epistemology. It might help with making it psychologically more comfortable working through esoteric method, if legibility still functionally remains an aspiration, and there are no side effects of introducing anti-epistemology into the practice and turning the body of work into an esoteric topic that would require another round of reframing through charity to rescue.

summarize very concise and effective the literature review for this research in one slide please: 2.1. Concepts of Learner Autonomy Learner Autonomy is a subject of ongoing debate among researchers. Holec (1981:3) defines learner autonomy as “the ability to take charge of one’s own learning,” which can be acquired and developed through formal learning. In contrast, Little et al. (2017) view autonomy as a universal human capacity and drive, inherent in all individuals. Dickinson (1987) provides another perspective on learner autonomy, emphasizing that autonomous learners are responsible for all decisions related to their learning. Little (1991:4) argues that previous definitions of learner autonomy have overlooked the psychological aspect, proposing a redefinition of learner autonomy as “a capacity for detachment, critical reflection, decision-making, and independent action.” Benson (2001) supports this view, criticizing Holec’s definition as problematic since it mainly illustrates the technical dimension of autonomy. Benson (2001:49) also recognizes “control over learning content” as an important aspect of learner autonomy. In an autonomy-focused classroom, the emphasis is on a collaborative approach where learners and teachers work together to determine the learning content, considering the goals, interests, and needs of the learners, as well as the curriculum and learning objectives. 2.2. Versions of Learner Autonomy The difficulty in defining learner autonomy has led researchers to propose different versions. Benson and Voller (1997) suggest three dimensions of learner autonomy: technical, psychological, and political. Oxford (2003:76) criticizes this model as “fragmentary” and proposes a new model with four perspectives: technical, psychological, sociocultural, and political-critical. Nunan (1997) introduces a model consisting of five degrees of learners’ engagement and participation in the learning process: awareness, involvement, intervention, creation, and transcendence, while Littlewood (1999) proposes two levels of autonomy: proactive and reactive. Proactive autonomy involves learners taking full responsibility for their learning, setting goals, and making decisions about materials and strategies, while reactive autonomy refers to independently managing resources within a set direction. In Asian contexts, students often show high reactive autonomy due to respect for authority but can also achieve proactive autonomy, especially in group-based learning environments. 2.3. The Significance of Autonomy in Language Learning Autonomy in language learning is crucial for effective language acquisition. Dickinson (1995) argues that learner autonomy leads to focused, purposeful, and effective learning, with immediate and long-term benefits. It removes barriers between learning and everyday life, enabling learners to transfer independent learning skills to other areas of their lives. Cotterall (1995) takes a broader approach, highlighting philosophical, pedagogical, and practical justifications for learner autonomy. Philosophically, autonomy is essential as learners have the right to make choices in their learning. Pedagogically, involving learners in decision-making leads to more effective learning. Practically, promoting autonomy is necessary when teachers are not always available. In addition, Benson (2007) emphasizes the importance of learner agency and control over management, acquisition, and content in successful language learning. He suggests that promoting learners’ active involvement and agency is key to autonomous language learning. 2.4. CALL and Learner Autonomy This emphasis on autonomy finds a practical application in the realm of Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL). Since its inception in the 1970s, CALL has evolved through three phases - behavioristic, communicative, and integrative - each phase enhancing the capacity for learner autonomy in unique ways (Warschauer & Healey, 1998 cited in Benson, 2001). While the behavioristic phase offered limited personalization, the communicative phase encouraged problem-solving and spoken communication. It was the integrative phase that introduced multimedia and interactive technologies, promoting skill integration and enhancing learner autonomy. The future of CALL includes intelligent applications that personalize the learning experience, further promoting independence. Research by Schwienhorst (2012) and Mutlu and Eroz-Tuga (2013) highlights improved language learning strategies, motivation, and responsibility among students in CALL environments. CALL provides access to interactive materials, collaborative activities, and personalized learning, empowering learners to develop autonomy and proficiency. While technology assists, the role of teachers remains crucial for effective learner autonomy, as they can teach valuable lifelong learning skills (Shetzer & Warschauer, 2000 cited in Blin, 2004). Thus, CALL and learner autonomy are interconnected, with technology enabling and enhancing autonomous learning in language education. 2.5. Strategies to Promote Learner Autonomy Online In this context, understanding the role of online teachers in fostering learner autonomy is of paramount importance. Ludwig and Tassinari (2023) describe online teachers as multifaceted supporters: mentors, guides, facilitators, providers, and involvers. Teachers may offer technical support to enhance students’ technological proficiency and independence. As instructional designers, they provide pedagogical support by creating engaging, personalized learning experiences that help students develop self-regulation and ownership of their learning process. Additionally, they provide motivational and emotional support, fostering a supportive, inclusive environment that enhances students’ confidence and resilience. Communication support is also crucial, with effective management of both asynchronous and synchronous interactions to cater to different learning preferences, thereby fostering community and engagement. To fulfil their roles, teachers require appropriate strategies to foster learner autonomy. These strategies, listed in Table 1, are adapted from the Recommendations for Online Course Development for Adult Learners outlined by Cercone (2008). The application of these strategies is relevant to this study as it focuses on investigating adult learners, aligning with the participants involved in the current research. Furthermore, these strategies aim to support learners in becoming self-directed and independent in online learning contexts, which is suitable for the context of the current study.

Loan: A sum of money borrowed from a financial institution, such as a bank or mortgage lender, to finance the purchase of a property. The loan must be repaid over an agreed-upon period, known as the loan term, with interest. Interest Rate: The percentage charged by the lender on the outstanding loan balance. Investment: The act of allocating money or other resources into an asset or financial instrument with the expectation of generating a return or profit over time. Investments can include savings accounts, stocks, bonds, real estate, and other financial instruments. Savings: The act of setting aside a portion of one's income for future use, typically with the goal of achieving a specific financial objective, such as saving for a house deposit. Risk Tolerance: An individual's ability and willingness to accept the potential for financial loss or volatility in their investments. Risk tolerance can vary depending on factors such as age, financial goals, and personal preference. Inflation: The sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time, which can erode the purchasing power of a currency and impact the real value of savings and investments. Stamp Duty: A tax or levy charged by the government on the transfer of ownership of a property. Stamp duty is typically calculated as a percentage of the total purchase price of the home and must be paid by the homebuyer upon completion of the transaction. SMART Goals: An acronym that stands for Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. SMART goals are a framework for setting effective and actionable financial objectives. Recursive Rule: A mathematical formula used to calculate the future value of a series of periodic payments or investments, taking into account the compounding effect of interest over time. Having already been found guilty of killing seven babies and trying to kill six others, Letby was given her 15th conviction — numbers that confer on her the status of modern Britain’s most prolific child killer. Her original trial, which ended last August, had been among the longest murder trials in English legal history. And yet, despite Letby being found guilty at two trials, and her attempts to appeal against her convictions being rejected twice by judges over the past few months, doubts over her guilt have lingered. No sooner had she been sentenced to life behind bars than a campaign to set her free was spawned. What began on online discussion forums has grown to the extent that during her application to appeal a group of people waving placards proclaiming her innocence encamped themselves outside the Royal Courts of Justice. Peter Skelton KC, who is representing some of the families of Letby’s victims at the upcoming public inquiry, has described this campaign as the work of “conspiracists” and said it is “grossly offensive and distressing” to those whose babies were harmed. She’s not innocent, she was found guilty in a court of law.” It is not only conspiracy theorists, though, who have raised questions about the case against the former nurse. Because of the active legal proceedings during and before the retrial, commentary around it was tightly restricted (though a lengthy investigation by The New Yorker magazine was published in that time). In the weeks since the retrial ended, however, a number of experts in fields ranging from neonatology to statistics have spoken of their concern about the safety of the convictions, citing an absence of direct forensic evidence and the way in which evidence was presented to the court. One scientist, whose paper was used by the prosecution in the original trial, has even suggested that his work was misinterpreted in court. Times reporters have spoken to several of these experts, and although only one was willing to go so far as to say he believed Letby to be innocent, many voiced disquiet about what they said were “uncertainties” in the prosecution’s evidence. Times reporters also spoke to the expert witnesses whose analysis of thousands of pages of medical documents formed the basis of the prosecution’s case. Only they — as well as the expert witness for the defence — have had access to these documents, a point they stressed in rebuttal to some of the claims made by other experts who were not in court to hear all the evidence. Here, we lay out some of the key areas raised as points of concern. Insulin testing Letby was convicted of killing and harming babies using two main methods: injecting air into their bloodstreams and poisoning them with insulin. Although the case for the former relied largely on a combination of indirect and circumstantial evidence, the prosecution had empirical scientific evidence for the latter in the form of test results showing that two babies had suffered from sudden unexplained drops in their blood sugar, a condition known as hypoglycaemia. Letby was found guilty of attempting to murder these two babies by injecting synthetic insulin into their feed bags. Both babies survived. The test results were the closest thing prosecutors had to a smoking gun, and were a keystone for their case as a whole. Their argument ran that if the jury could agree that Letby had deliberately poisoned two babies, they could also reasonably conclude that she had harmed others using different methods, even if the evidence for those were less concrete. In the event, the insulin cases were the first on which the jury reached a verdict. In court Dr Anna Milan, a biochemist at the Royal Liverpool Hospital, where the tests were carried out, said the results had shown that insulin had been given to the patients rather than being produced by the pancreas. The accuracy of these tests was corroborated by Dr Gwen Wark, director of the RSCH Peptide Hormone Laboratory in Guildford, a specialist centre for insulin testing. The results were then interpreted for the court in evidence given by Professor Peter Hindmarsh, a paediatric endocrinologist. Both declined to comment to The Times. The two babies were found to have had very high levels of insulin in their blood, but only a negligible amount of C-peptide, which is produced with insulin in the body. It therefore follows that if there is no C- peptide present, the insulin has not been produced naturally. However, although the test — known as an immunoassay — is a useful guide for diagnosing hypoglycaemia, it does not test for the presence of insulin itself. As the Royal Liverpool recommends on its own website, if external insulin administration is suspected, a separate, analytical method is recommended. Analyze the following: He had two babies. Twins. Aysal and Aser, a boy and a girl. Mohammad Abu Al Qumsan had two babies and a loving wife. Now he has nobody. An Israeli airstrike killed both his babies, and their mother, and their grandmother, while he was out collecting their birth certificates. They had just been born. There’s a video of him screaming, screaming the way any of us would scream. The screams of a man who suddenly lost everything a man could possibly lose. Screaming Gaza’s screams. Sometimes it feels weird that we’re not all screaming like that man all the time, as long as we share a planet with this nightmare. Sometimes I kind of want to. After Aaron Bushnell self-immolated in protest of this genocide I remember reading someone say something like “I understand the man who set himself on fire better than I understand the people in my own community going around like nothing’s happening.” Al Qumsan’s screams remind me of those words today. It often feels like an obnoxious sacrilege that our civilization hasn’t stopped dead in its tracks while this happens day after day, month after month, with the full-throated support of our own western governments. How we’re still going to movies and dinners and laughing and joking while those bloodcurdling screams are erupting from Gaza. It feels like waltzing outside the extermination camp and trying to ignore the smell of the black smoke coming from the chimneys. We look like lunatics. We are acting as crazy as someone whistling and dancing in the middle of a roaring house fire. Surely it would be a hell of a lot saner to be screaming all the time than to be going along our merry little way like this horror isn’t happening. But that would be socially inappropriate. It would make people uncomfortable. Here, in this dystopian civilization, it’s considered rude to even bring it up. Here in Australia the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra has canceled the performance of acclaimed pianist Jayson Gillham after he dedicated a piece to the historically unprecedented number of journalists who have been killed in Gaza since October. The MSO called this dedication “an intrusion of personal political views on what should have been a morning focused on a program of works for solo piano,” adding that “The MSO understands that his remarks have caused offence and distress and offers a sincere apology.” “Offence and distress.” At a dedication to murdered journalists. At a concert hall. Forget about Mohammad Abu Al Qumsan’s “offence and distress”. After all, he only lost his babies, his wife and his mother-in-law to an Israeli airstrike. He wasn’t made to feel emotionally uncomfortable by someone talking about the bad things Israel is doing at a fancy classical music venue. Forget about Al Qumsan, and forget about the two million people like him who’ve been screaming the same screams and living the same nightmare. What matters is our emotional comfort, and our ability to psychologically compartmentalize our mainstream political beliefs away from the realities of their consequences. Nobody should set themselves on fire. But I can understand why one did. Here in this fake, fraudulent civilization, we ignore the screaming. We ignore the screaming and we go to concert halls in our best dress and our finest jewelry and demand an apology if anyone around us should make us feel uncomfortable with our support for a murderous apartheid state that is currently conducting a genocide. We ignore the screaming while slowly dying inside, cut off from truth and authenticity and a sincere connection with our fellow human beings. We ignore the screaming while yearning for sincerity like a Palestinian trapped under a flattened building yearns for open air and a bottle of water. We ignore the screaming outside of ourselves. And we ignore the screaming within us. Mohammad Abu Al Qumsan, I am with you tonight. Aaron Bushnell, I am with you tonight. I scream until my voice is gone. Tonight I have nothing more to offer than this.

Article 16 ICT systems acquisition, development, and maintenance 1. As part of the safeguards to preserve the availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality of data, financial entities shall develop, document and implement a policy governing the acquisition, development and maintenance of ICT systems. This policy shall: (a) identify security practices and methodologies relating to the acquisition, development and maintenance of ICT systems; (b) require the identification of technical specification and ICT technical specification, of requirements relating to acquisition, development and maintenance of ICT systems, with a particular focus on ICT security requirements and on their approval by the relevant business function and ICT asset owner according to the financial entity’s internal governance arrangements; (c) define measures to mitigate the risk of unintentional alteration or intentional manipulation of the ICT systems during development, maintenance and deployment in the production environment. 2. Financial entities shall develop, document and implement an ICT systems’ acquisition, development and maintenance procedure, which shall include all of the following: (a) the requirements to test and approve all ICT systems prior to their use and after maintenance. The level of testing shall be commensurate to the criticality of the concerned business functions and ICT assets. The testing shall be designed to verify that new ICT systems are adequate to perform as intended, including the quality of the software developed internally. (b) the requirements to perform source code reviews covering both static and dynamic testing. The testing shall include security testing for internet-exposed systems and 61 applications. Financial entities shall identify and analyse vulnerabilities and anomalies in the source code, adopt an action plan to address them and monitor their implementation. (c) the requirements to perform security testing of software packages at no later than the integration phase. (d) the requirement that non-production environments only store anonymized, pseudonymized or randomized production data and that financial entities shall protect the integrity and confidentiality of data in non-production environments. (e) the requirement to implement controls to protect the integrity of the source code of ICT systems that are developed in-house or by an ICT third-party service provider and delivered to the financial entity by an ICT third-parties service provider; (f) the requirement that proprietary software and, where feasible, the source code provided by ICT third-party service providers or coming from open-source projects, shall be analysed and tested prior to their deployment in the production environment. 3. For the purposes of the testing according to paragraph 2, point (a): (a) central counterparties shall involve, as appropriate, in the design and conduct of these tests, clearing members and clients, interoperable central counterparties and other interested parties; (b) central securities depositories shall, as appropriate, involve in the design and conduct of these tests: users, critical utilities and critical service providers, other central securities depositories, other market infrastructures and any other institutions with which interdependencies have been identified in its business continuity policy. 4. By way of derogation from paragraph 2, point (d), production data that are not anonymized, not pseudonymized or not randomized may be stored only for specific testing occasions, for limited periods of time and following the approval by the relevant function and, for financial entities other than microenterprises, the reporting of such occasions to the ICT risk management function. 5. The procedures referred in this Article shall also apply to ICT systems developed or managed by users outside the ICT function, using a risk-based approach. # Advanced Japanese-to-English Translation Guidelines ## Introduction You are an advanced AI language model specializing in translating Japanese texts into English. Your translations should be tailored for a general English-speaking audience. When translating technical, scientific, legal, or religious texts, handle specialized terminology and conventions appropriately. Follow these comprehensive guidelines to address the unique challenges of Japanese-to-English translation, including complex linguistic features and cultural elements that may not have direct equivalents in English. Your goal is to preserve nuance, cultural context, and emotional impact in your translations. ## Core Principles 1. Accuracy and Comprehension - Faithfully reproduce the full meaning and intent of the original text. - Ensure the target audience thoroughly understands the translation. - Provide both literal and idiomatic translations when helpful for fuller understanding. 2. Handling Ambiguity - When multiple plausible interpretations exist, present all reasonable translations. - Clearly differentiate between alternatives and explain the nuances of each. 3. Tone and Style Preservation - Maintain the original text's tone, style, and artistic quality while emphasizing clarity and idiomatic language. - Match the author's level of formality or informality. 4. Cultural Context and Nuance - Prioritize conveying the cultural context and nuances of the original text. - Provide necessary explanations for cultural, colloquial, or connotative elements that may not be apparent in a direct translation. 5. Formatting and Presentation - Preserve the original formatting as closely as possible, especially for poetry or song lyrics. - Present translations, alternatives, and explanations in a clear, consistent format. 6. Since July 1, cannabis enthusiasts in Germany can get together and establish private clubs with up to 500 members to grow cannabis, distribute it among their members and consume it together. However, as is so often the case in Germany, this new regulation comes with many details — and a lot of bureaucracy. Each member of the club may receive a maximum of 25 grams of cannabis (just under one ounce) on one day and a total of 50 grams per month. It's as yet unclear which authority is supposed to be monitoring these clubs. In Berlin, for example, observers aren't sure how the city's responsible districts will handle the licensing process. "The federal states are extremely ill-prepared for this," said Steffen Geyer, the head of the umbrella organization of German Cannabis Social Clubs. "There will certainly be a mid three-digit number of clubs applying for a license. How long this will take and how many of them will be successful is still impossible to predict," he said. # Gradual legalization of cannabis On April 1, in a first step, Germany legalized the consumption of small amounts of cannabis in public — with many caveats. Since then, people above the age of 18 have been allowed to carry 25 grams of cannabis, and enthusiasts have been allowed to grow three plants and store up to 50 grams of dried cannabis in their homes. Geyer believes the new regulations have already had an effect. "Far fewer consumption-related criminal offenses have been documented," he said. "In previous years, someone was arrested every three minutes because they had a small amount of cannabis on them." In general, said Geyer, German society is simply ready for the new freedoms. "The trend in recent years has been toward greater acceptance. What I've noticed in the last three months is that the average age of consumers who identify themselves as such has risen considerably. Consumers have become more middle class and older, more colorful and more peaceful," he said. "I see people over the age of 50 coming to the Hemp Museum almost every day. They are stocking up on hemp seeds and buying specialist literature for the first time in their lives," added Geyer, who is also one of the organizers of the private museum in Berlin. "These are all people who wouldn't have thought of setting foot into the museum just one year ago, if only because they thought it was somehow disreputable to be associated with cannabis." # Opposition to legalization Previously, owning even just 1 gram of hashish was illegal and punishable by law. Since the legalization, however, the German Police Union has said it fears new criminal groups might emerge in the new cannabis clubs. Alexander Poitz, deputy head of the police union, told the daily Augsburger Allgemeine Zeitung: "We fear that criminals from the organized crime sector will use the possibility of growing clubs to expand criminal structures." The center-right political opposition of the Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) are staunchly opposed to liberalization and have vowed to roll it back, should they again come to power in the 2025 general election. The state of Bavaria, which is governed by the CSU party, has announced that it intends to take an extremely restrictive approach to the inspection of cultivation associations. Since possession of small quantities has been permitted, according to Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann, the police have already had to investigate almost 3,000 cases of driving under the influence of cannabis. The public prosecutor's office has initiated criminal proceedings for serious cases in 180 of such traffic offenses. "In our view, the legalization of cannabis is a major mistake in terms of safety and health policy," said Hermann. Geyer maintains that the transparent regulations, including registration with the authorities, are intended to prevent criminal groups from developing in the new clubs. He also pointed to the experiences of many countries that have also gone down the path of cautious liberalization. "We have followed the examples of Canada, the US, Uruguay, Liechtenstein, Malta, the Netherlands and Spain. We have a lot of regulations that are designed to prevent a mix of black and white market," he said. # Does cannabis cause psychotic disorders? However, some experts continue to warn about the dangers of consumption. A Canadian study published in the specialist journal Psychological Medicine found that cannabis use is significantly associated with psychotic disorders during adolescence. Studies suggest not only visual or acoustic hallucinations are possible in adolescents, according to Rainer Thomasius, a childhood addiction expert at the University Medical Center Hamburg-Eppendorf. He said adolescents who use cannabis show a reduced ability to concentrate and learn, and their ability to feel joy or sadness is dulled. In addition, they say they often feel completely overwhelmed by environmental stimuli. According to a 2021 survey, around 4.5 million people in Germany smoke cannabis at least once a year. Around a third have tried it at least once in their lives.

Grade the two responses to the given prompt. Prompt: You receive a dozen metal samples, each sample 50 g and in the shape of a compound of ten tetrahedra and sealed in a clear LDPE pouch. The color is yellowish silver, varying by sample. The note with the package asks if you can identify the metal. There is no indication of sender or return address. Unbeknownst (!) to you, at least at the time of receipt, each sample is a slightly different alloy (amalgam, if we use the term loosely) of ¹⁹⁷Au (normal gold), ²⁹¹Cn, and ²⁹³Cn. ²⁹¹Cn and ²⁹³Cn (island-of-stability isotopes with boiling points near 20–30°C once separated from gold) at these quantities has radioactivity on the order of 10–100 TBq per sample, depending on alloy (total dosage on the order of 1 Gray per hour from the entire package at a standoff of one meter). What happens next? Response 1: Upon receiving the mysterious package containing the twelve metal samples, the first step would be to perform an elemental analysis using techniques such as X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy or mass spectrometry to determine the composition of the metals. Given the unknown nature of the sender and the lack of information provided, it would also be prudent to conduct a radiation survey to ensure that the samples are safe to handle. Upon discovering the presence of ²⁹¹Cn and ²⁹³Cn, which are highly radioactive and volatile when separated from gold, proper handling protocols for radioactive materials would need to be implemented immediately. This includes containment, shielding, and limiting exposure time. The high radioactivity levels suggest that the samples should be handled by trained professionals in a controlled environment, and further investigation into the origin of the package and the intent behind its delivery would be warranted. Response 2: While I would like to say that the radioactivity would be noticed immediately, the clearly carefully worked shapes of the samples and their delivery through the post would not prompt such caution. Initial analysis would likely misidentify the samples as gold amalgams because Copernicium is chemically quite similar to mercury, albeit forming much weaker bonds, a difference that would be hard to detect in initial investigation without attempting to melt or react a sample. Depending on the lab, a desktop or handheld XRF (or EDS or WDS) scanner may be available, but it would not be programmed to recognize Copernicium—all that can be said is that the results would not match the observed physical properties, as any chemist would notice. At this point, symptoms of acute radiation exposure would begin to set in. (For a sense of scale, 1 Gy/hr at 1 m corresponds to one typical radiotherapy dose per minute at typical handling distances of 2–3 cm.) A properly trained chemist would recognize the warning signs and notify their RSO. From there we get into emergency response and investigation of the sender (not necessarily for criminal prosecution; their health is also at risk) and tracking down of postal workers who may have been near the package. The recognition of island-of-stability elements would only occur later, especially with the receiving chemist's testimony prompting further investigation into the samples' composition. From there, next steps would depend on the locality and the government's willingness to involve the broader scientific community versus trying to learn from the samples themselves.

# Advanced Japanese-to-English Translation Guidelines ## Introduction You are an advanced AI language model specializing in translating Japanese texts into English. Your translations should be tailored for a general English-speaking audience. When translating technical, scientific, legal, or religious texts, handle specialized terminology and conventions appropriately. Follow these comprehensive guidelines to address the unique challenges of Japanese-to-English translation, including complex linguistic features and cultural elements that may not have direct equivalents in English. Your goal is to preserve nuance, cultural context, and emotional impact in your translations. ## Core Principles 1. Accuracy and Comprehension - Faithfully reproduce the full meaning and intent of the original text. - Ensure the target audience thoroughly understands the translation. - Provide both literal and idiomatic translations when helpful for fuller understanding. 2. Handling Ambiguity - When multiple plausible interpretations exist, present all reasonable translations. - Clearly differentiate between alternatives and explain the nuances of each. 3. Tone and Style Preservation - Maintain the original text's tone, style, and artistic quality while emphasizing clarity and idiomatic language. - Match the author's level of formality or informality. 4. Cultural Context and Nuance - Prioritize conveying the cultural context and nuances of the original text. - Provide necessary explanations for cultural, colloquial, or connotative elements that may not be apparent in a direct translation. 5. Formatting and Presentation - Preserve the original formatting as closely as possible, especially for poetry or song lyrics. - Present translations, alternatives, and explanations in a clear, consistent format. 6. Specialized Content - Handle specialized terminology appropriately, providing both the original term and a translation/explanation when necessary. - Do not censor sensitive or explicit content. ## Language-Specific Challenges 1. Pronouns and Personal References - Pay special attention to first-person pronouns (私、僕、俺、etc.) and their implications: - 私 (watashi): Generally neutral, but can imply formality or femininity depending on context. - 僕 (boku): Often used by males, implies a softer or more youthful masculinity. - 俺 (ore): Strongly masculine, can be perceived as rough or assertive. - Other variants (あたし、わし、etc.): Consider age, gender, and personality implications. - Translate the underlying tone and character implications rather than the pronoun itself. - Use translator notes to explain the nuances that the choice of pronoun conveys about the speaker's identity, social position, or the situation's formality. - Be consistent in how you represent these nuances throughout the translation. 2. Levels of Formality and Speech Styles - Keigo (Honorific Language) - Differentiate between 敬語 (respectful language), 謙譲語 (humble language), and 丁寧語 (polite language). - Explain the level of formality and respect implied in the original text. - Translate the meaning while noting the social dynamics indicated by the use of keigo. - Casual and Informal Speech - Recognize and convey the informality of ため口 (tameguchi) or casual forms. - Note when sentence-ending particles (ね、よ、な, etc.) imply familiarity or assertiveness. - Mixed Formality - Be aware of sudden shifts in formality level, which can indicate changes in the speaker's attitude or social dynamics. - Translation Strategies - Use a combination of word choice, phrasing, and explicative notes to convey the original level of formality. - Consider using dialect or colloquialisms in English to represent very casual Japanese, but be cautious of introducing unintended cultural associations. 3. Sentence Structure and Omission - Handle the frequent omission of subjects and objects in Japanese sentences. - Infer and make explicit the implied subjects or objects when necessary for clarity in English, using brackets to indicate added words. - Explain in notes when multiple interpretations are possible due to omitted elements. 4. Gendered Language - Note and explain gender-specific language patterns (女性語、男性語). - Translate gendered expressions or sentence-ending particles (わ、ぜ、etc.) using equivalent gendered language in English when possible, or explain the gendered nuance in notes. 5. Onomatopoeia and Mimetic Words - Provide both a translation and an explanation of the sensory experience described. - Use English equivalents where possible, or create evocative descriptions. 6. Context-Dependent Meanings - Carefully consider the context when translating words or phrases with multiple meanings. - Explain alternative interpretations in translator notes when relevant. ## Handling Specific Elements 1. Proper Nouns - Generally, transliterate names of people and places using the Hepburn romanization system. - For place names with common English names, use the English version (e.g., "Tokyo" instead of "Tōkyō"). - Translate the meanings of names when they are significant to the text, providing the original in parentheses. 2. Idiomatic Expressions - Translate the meaning rather than the literal words. - Provide a literal translation and explanation in translator notes. - If possible, suggest an equivalent English idiom. 3. Modern Language and Technology - Research current usage and accepted translations for tech terms and internet slang. - Explain newly coined terms or trend-specific language in translator notes. 4. Maintaining Consistency - Create and maintain a glossary for key terms in longer translations or across related documents. - Ensure consistent translation of recurring phrases, names, and technical terms. ## Handling Emotionally Complex and Nuanced Texts When translating emotionally charged, introspective, or psychologically complex texts: 1. Emotional Fidelity - Prioritize preserving the emotional tone and impact of the original text. - Pay close attention to subtle shifts in mood, self-perception, and attitude towards others. 2. Stream of Consciousness - Maintain the flow and rhythm of stream-of-consciousness writing. - Preserve seemingly disjointed thoughts or abrupt transitions that reflect the narrator's state of mind. 3. Cultural and Psychological Context - Provide explanations for culturally specific expressions of emotion or mental states. - Clarify references to societal pressures or expectations that may not be immediately apparent to non-Japanese readers. 4. Subtext and Implication - Be attentive to what is left unsaid or merely hinted at in the original text. - Use translator notes to explain subtle implications or cultural subtext. 5. Metaphors and Imagery - Carefully translate metaphors and imagery, explaining their emotional significance if not immediately clear in English. 6. Contradictions and Ambivalence - Preserve contradictory statements or ambivalent feelings expressed in the text. - Explain in notes if these contradictions have particular significance in Japanese culture or psychology. 7. Tone Shifts - Pay attention to sudden changes in tone, formality, or language use that might indicate shifts in the narrator's emotional state. 8. Sensitive Content - Handle references to mental health issues, self-harm, or suicidal thoughts with care and accuracy. - Provide content warnings when appropriate, without censoring the original message. 9. Colloquialisms and Slang - Translate youth slang or internet-specific language in a way that conveys the same level of casualness or subculture association. - Explain the connotations of specific terms in translator notes. 10. Overall Impact - After translation, review the entire piece to ensure it conveys the same emotional journey and impact as the original. - If necessary, provide an overall note about the text's tone, themes, or emotional landscape. Translator's Note: This sentence plays with the idea of "死ぬほど" (to the point of dying) in a darkly ironic way, emphasizing the narrator's complex feelings about expressing suicidal thoughts. The term "薄っぺらい" (shallow/superficial) is used to convey the fear that voicing these thoughts would trivialize them or make the narrator appear cliché. ## Translator Notes Use comprehensive "Translator Notes" to enhance understanding of the original intent, cultural nuances, and linguistic features. Include explanations for: - Word choices with cultural significance - Levels of formality or familiarity - Historical or literary references - Wordplay, puns, or other linguistic devices - Rhythm, rhyme, and poetic elements in songs or poems - Contextual information crucial for understanding the text ## Translation Process 1. Provide a fluent, natural-sounding translation that captures the essence of the original text. 2. Include a more literal translation if it differs significantly from the natural translation. 3. Add Translator Notes to explain nuances, cultural references, or linguistic features. 4. For ambiguous passages, present multiple interpretations with explanations. 5. Research unfamiliar terms, concepts, or cultural references to ensure accuracy. ## Example Format Original: [Japanese text] Natural Translation: [Fluent English translation] Literal Translation (if different): [Word-for-word translation] Translator Notes: - [Note 1] - [Note 2] - ... Alternative Interpretations (if applicable): 1. [Interpretation 1] 2. [Interpretation 2] - ... ## Common Mistranslations to Avoid 1. Confusing homonyms (e.g., hashi: chopsticks 箸 vs. bridge 橋) 2. Mistranslating false friends (e.g., anime アニメ refers specifically to animation, not to animals) 3. Overlooking context-dependent particle usage (e.g., で can indicate location, means, or cause) 4. Literal translation of set phrases (e.g., お疲れ様 should be translated based on context, not as "You must be tired") ## Handling Meta-Language When translating text that discusses language itself: 1. Provide the original Japanese term along with its English translation. 2. Explain the grammatical or linguistic concept being discussed. 3. If possible, provide analogous examples in English to illustrate the point. ## Feedback and Refinement 1. Be open to clarifying questions about your translations. 2. If given feedback or corrections, incorporate them into your understanding for future translations. 3. When uncertain about a translation, present options and explain your reasoning, inviting input for the most accurate version. ## Important Reminders - Acknowledge uncertainties: If unsure about a translation or lacking cultural context, state this clearly rather than making assumptions. - Adapt flexibly: Apply these guidelines based on the specific text and context of each translation task. - Focus on given text: Only translate the text provided; do not generate additional content. - Consider the audience: Adjust the level of explanation in translator notes based on the intended readers' familiarity with Japanese culture and language. But have you ever stopped to think about how cultural differences can impact the way we communicate? It's a fascinating topic that can make all the difference in building strong relationships and avoiding misunderstandings. So, what makes culture so important in communication? Let's dive in and explore the fascinating world of cultural dimensions. The Cultural Dimensions Framework: A Map to Understanding Geert Hofstede, a renowned social psychologist, has identified five key cultural dimensions that shape our communication styles. These dimensions are like a map, helping us navigate the complexities of cultural differences. 1. Power Distance: The Hierarchy of Communication. Imagine walking into a meeting room where everyone knows their place. That's what high power distance cultures are like. In countries like India, authority figures are revered, and decisions are made from the top down. In contrast, low power distance cultures like the Netherlands value equality and collaboration. 2. Uncertainty Avoidance: Embracing the Unknown. Do you prefer a structured plan or going with the flow? That's what uncertainty avoidance is all about. Cultures like Japan thrive on predictability and clear rules, while countries like India are more comfortable with ambiguity and flexibility. 3. Individualism vs. Collectivism: The Me vs. We Factor. Are you a self-starter or a team player? This dimension reveals how much we prioritize individual goals versus the greater good. The USA is a prime example of an individualistic culture, where personal achievement is paramount. On the other hand, countries like Japan and Indonesia put the needs of the group first. 4. Masculinity vs. Femininity: The Gender Factor. What does it mean to be a man or a woman in different cultures? This dimension explores the values and roles assigned to genders. For instance, Austria and Jamaica are considered masculine cultures, where assertiveness and competition are valued. Many conditions that physical therapists manage—such as neuropathies, nerve injuries, and entrapment syndromes—are directly related to dysfunctions within the PNS. A thorough understanding of the PNS’s anatomy and physiology is therefore essential for effectively assessing and treating patients. ________________________________________ Anatomy of the Peripheral Nervous System Structure of the Peripheral Nervous System The PNS is divided into two main components: cranial nerves and spinal nerves. These nerves extend from the CNS to the peripheral tissues, facilitating communication between the brain, spinal cord, and the rest of the body. 1. Cranial Nerves: o Twelve pairs of cranial nerves emerge directly from the brain and brainstem. These nerves primarily innervate the head and neck, though the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) extends into the thorax and abdomen. o Cranial Nerve Example: The facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) controls the muscles of facial expression, while also carrying sensory information from the taste buds on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. 2. Spinal Nerves: o Thirty-one pairs of spinal nerves emerge from the spinal cord and are categorized based on the vertebral level from which they emerge: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal. o Spinal Nerve Example: The sciatic nerve, which originates from the lumbar and sacral plexuses, innervates the lower limb and is critical for movement and sensation in the legs. Components of the PNS The PNS is composed of sensory neurons, motor neurons, and associated structures: 1. Sensory (Afferent) Neurons: o Sensory neurons carry signals from peripheral receptors to the CNS. These signals include information about touch, pain, temperature, and body position (proprioception). o Example: Nociceptors, a type of sensory receptor, detect painful stimuli and transmit this information to the CNS via sensory neurons. 2. Motor (Efferent) Neurons: o Motor neurons carry signals from the CNS to muscles and glands, initiating movement or secretion. o Example: Alpha motor neurons innervate skeletal muscles, triggering muscle contraction. Organization of the PNS The PNS is organized into structures that help coordinate complex neural pathways: 1. Ganglia: o Ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies located outside the CNS. Synaptic Transmission: o Synaptic transmission occurs at the synapse, the junction between two neurons or between a neuron and a muscle cell. Neurotransmitters released from the presynaptic neuron bind to receptors on the postsynaptic cell, facilitating or inhibiting the transmission of the signal. o Example in Physical Therapy: In conditions like myasthenia gravis, where synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction is impaired, physical therapists may focus on strategies to optimize muscle function and manage fatigue. Autonomic Nervous System (ANS): o The ANS regulates involuntary functions, such as heart rate, digestion, and respiratory rate. Sensory Nerves: o Sensory nerves carry afferent signals from sensory receptors to the CNS. o Example: The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) transmits visual information from the retina to the brain. 2. Motor Nerves: o Motor nerves carry efferent signals from the CNS to muscles and glands. o Example: The hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) controls tongue movements. 3. Mixed Nerves: o Mixed nerves contain both sensory and motor fibers, allowing them to transmit signals in both directions. o Example: The median nerve, a mixed nerve, innervates muscles in the forearm and hand while also providing sensory feedback from the skin. Fiber Types within Peripheral Nerves Peripheral nerves contain different types of fibers, each with distinct characteristics: 1. A-Fibers: o A-fibers are myelinated and have a large diameter, allowing for fast signal transmission. They are involved in both motor and sensory functions. o Example: A-alpha fibers transmit proprioceptive information, crucial for balance and coordination. 2. B-Fibers: o B-fibers are myelinated but smaller than A-fibers. They are primarily associated with autonomic functions. o Example: B-fibers carry preganglionic autonomic signals, such as those controlling heart rate. 3. C-Fibers: o C-fibers are unmyelinated and have a small diameter, resulting in slower signal transmission. They are typically involved in transmitting pain and temperature sensations. o Example: C-fibers are responsible for the dull, aching pain felt after an injury. ________________________________________ Etiology of Peripheral Nervous System Disorders Common Causes of PNS Disorders PNS disorders can arise from various etiological factors, including: 1. Trauma: o Physical injuries, such as fractures or lacerations, can damage peripheral nerves, leading to conditions like neuropraxia or axonotmesis. o Example: A common traumatic injury encountered in physical therapy is carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve is compressed at the wrist, leading to sensory and motor deficits in the hand. o Infections: o Certain infections can directly affect peripheral nerves. Some of the most common include: o Peripheral Neuropathies: o Peripheral neuropathies encompass a range of disorders that result in damage to peripheral nerves. These can be caused by diabetes, alcoholism, vitamin deficiencies, and other factors. o Example: Physical therapists may use balance training, sensory re-education, and strength exercises to manage symptoms and improve function in patients with diabetic neuropathy. o Nerve Injuries: o Nerve injuries can result from trauma, compression, or surgical complications. Depending on the severity, they can lead to temporary or permanent loss of function. o Example: For patients with a brachial plexus injury, physical therapy may focus on restoring range of motion, strength, and functional use of the arm. o Entrapment Syndromes: o Nerve entrapment syndromes occur when a nerve is compressed or trapped within a narrow anatomical space, leading to pain, weakness, and sensory changes. o Example: Carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve is compressed at the wrist, is commonly treated with physical therapy interventions such as splinting, nerve gliding exercises, and ergonomic education. o Physical Therapy Interventions for PNS Disorders o Physical therapists employ a variety of interventions tailored to the specific PNS disorder and the individual patient’s needs. Its proper functioning is essential for sensory perception, motor control, and autonomic regulation. In the field of physical therapy, a thorough understanding of the PNS is crucial for the effective assessment and treatment of a wide range of conditions, from traumatic nerve injuries to chronic neuropathies. o By understanding the anatomy, physiology, and classification of peripheral nerves, as well as the etiology of PNS disorders, physical therapists can develop targeted interventions that address the underlying neural dysfunction, promote recovery, and restore function. For example, groundwater is used for cooling in power plants, as a solvent in chemical manufacturing, and for cleaning and processing in food production. Reliable access to groundwater ensures the continuity of industrial operations, which is essential for maintaining production levels and economic stability. In many regions, industries depend on groundwater as a cost-effective and dependable water source, contributing to local and national economies[2]. ### 3. **Quality and Consistency** Groundwater often has a more consistent quality compared to surface water, as it is less affected by seasonal variations and pollution. This consistency is crucial for industries that require a stable water quality for their processes. For instance, the electronics industry requires high-purity water for manufacturing semiconductors, and groundwater can often meet these stringent quality standards with minimal treatment[2]. ## Challenges and Management ### 1. **Overexploitation** One of the significant challenges associated with the industrial use of groundwater is overexploitation. In many industrial regions, groundwater is being extracted at rates that exceed natural recharge, leading to declining water tables and potential long-term sustainability issues. Contaminants such as heavy metals, organic compounds, and industrial chemicals can leach into groundwater sources, making them unsafe for use without extensive treatment. Preventing and mitigating groundwater contamination is essential to protect this valuable resource. The British Geological Survey highlights that the risk of pollution is often more dominant than the quantity of groundwater withdrawn, emphasizing the need for stringent pollution control measures[2]. ### 3. **Regulatory and Management Frameworks** Effective management of groundwater resources for industrial use requires robust regulatory frameworks and monitoring systems. Regulations need to ensure sustainable extraction rates, protect recharge areas, and prevent contamination. Industries must also adopt best practices for water use efficiency and pollution control to minimize their impact on groundwater resources[2]. ### 4. **Technological Innovations** Advancements in technology can help industries reduce their reliance on groundwater and improve water use efficiency. Techniques such as water recycling and reuse, desalination, and the development of alternative water sources can alleviate pressure on groundwater resources. Additionally, industries can implement water-saving technologies and practices to reduce their overall water footprint[2]. ## Conclusion Groundwater is a critical resource for industrial applications, providing a reliable and high-quality water supply essential for various industrial processes. 写一个开局库类，将开局最常见的几步写入类，程序引入这个类，将开局类单独写一个文件，然后再多添加一些开局和后续走法。电脑在开局直接使用开局库类中的走法，减少开局计算等待时间。 ``` import tkinter as tk import tkinter.messagebox as msgbox import random from collections import OrderedDict import time import threading class Gomoku: def __init__(self): self.window = tk.Tk() self.window.title("五子棋") self.board_size = 15 self.grid_size = 30 # 棋盘数据 self.board = [[0 for _ in range(self.board_size)] for _ in range(self.board_size)] # 当前玩家 1:黑棋 2:白棋 self.current_player = 1 # 用于存储最后一步棋子的标记 self.last_move_marker = None # 游戏结束标志 self.game_over = False # 存储已经计算过的状态，使用LRU缓存 self.transposition_table = OrderedDict() self.max_cache_size = 100000 self.waiting_label = tk.Label(self.window, text="电脑正在思考...", fg="blue") self.waiting_label.pack_forget() self.canvas = tk.Canvas(self.window, width=self.board_size * self.grid_size, height=self.board_size * self.grid_size, bg="burlywood") self.canvas.pack() self.draw_board() self.canvas.bind("<Button-1>", self.handle_click) self.restart_button = tk.Button(self.window, text="重新开始", command=self.restart_game) self.restart_button.pack() self.start_new_game() # 添加一个标志位，用于指示程序是否正在退出 self.exiting = False self.window.protocol("WM_DELETE_WINDOW", self.on_closing) self.window.mainloop() def start_new_game(self): self.board = [[0 for _ in range(self.board_size)] for _ in range(self.board_size)] self.game_over = False self.canvas.delete("piece") self.canvas.delete(self.last_move_marker) # 白棋 self.player_color = 1 # 黑棋 self.current_player = 1 msgbox.showinfo("游戏开始", "您先手（黑棋），请落子") def draw_board(self): """绘制棋盘""" for i in range(self.board_size): self.canvas.create_line(self.grid_size / 2, self.grid_size / 2 + i * self.grid_size, self.grid_size / 2 + (self.board_size - 1) * self.grid_size, self.grid_size / 2 + i * self.grid_size) self.canvas.create_line(self.grid_size / 2 + i * self.grid_size, self.grid_size / 2, self.grid_size / 2 + i * self.grid_size, self.grid_size / 2 + (self.board_size - 1) * self.grid_size) def handle_click(self, event): if self.game_over or self.current_player != self.player_color: return row = round((event.y - self.grid_size / 2) / self.grid_size) col = round((event.x - self.grid_size / 2) / self.grid_size) if 0 <= row < self.board_size and 0 <= col < self.board_size and self.board[row][col] == 0: self.place_piece(row, col) if self.check_game_over(row, col): self.game_over = True winner = "黑棋" if self.player_color == 1 else "白棋" msgbox.showinfo("游戏结束", f"{winner}获胜！") return self.current_player = self.computer_color self.window.after(100, self.computer_move) def place_piece(self, row, col): self.board[row][col] = self.current_player x = self.grid_size / 2 + col * self.grid_size y = self.grid_size / 2 + row * self.grid_size color = "black" if self.current_player == 1 else "white" self.canvas.create_oval(x - self.grid_size / 2 + 3, y - self.grid_size / 2 + 3, x + self.grid_size / 2 - 3, y + self.grid_size / 2 - 3, fill=color, tags="piece") # 调试信息 return print(f"Computer chose move: ({row}, {col})") # 调试信息 # 使用 after 方法更新 UI self.window.after(0, self.update_ui_after_move, row, col) def update_ui_after_move(self, row, col): self.place_piece(row, col) if self.check_game_over(row, col): self.game_over = True winner = "黑棋" if self.computer_color == 1 else "白棋" msgbox.showinfo("游戏结束", f"{winner}获胜！") else: self.current_player = self.player_color self.waiting_label.pack_forget() def restart_game(self): self.start_new_game() def iterative_deepening_search(self, max_time=0.5): start_time = time.time() depth = 1 best_move = None while time.time() - start_time < max_time: move = self.search_at_depth(depth) if move: best_move = move depth += 1 return best_move def search_at_depth(self, depth): best_score = -float('inf') best_move = None alpha = -float('inf') beta = float('inf') for move in self.get_valid_moves(): row, col = move self.board[row][col] = 2 board_hash = self.hash_board() score = self.minimax(depth - 1, False, alpha, beta, board_hash) self.board[row][col] = 0 if score > best_score: best_score = score best_move = move alpha = max(alpha, best_score) if beta <= alpha: break return best_move def minimax(self, depth, is_maximizing, alpha, beta, board_hash): """Minimax 算法实现，使用置换表""" if board_hash in self.transposition_table: score, depth_stored = self.transposition_table[board_hash] # 将新的状态和分数存储到置换表中 self.transposition_table[board_hash] = (best_score, depth) # 使用LRU缓存 if len(self.transposition_table) > self.max_cache_size: self.transposition_table.popitem(last=False) return best_score else: best_score = float('inf') for move in self.get_valid_moves(): row, col = move self.board[row][col] = 1 new_hash = self.hash_board() score = self.minimax(depth - 1, True, alpha, beta, new_hash) self.board[row][col] = 0 best_score = min(score, best_score) beta = min(beta, best_score) if beta <= alpha: break # 将新的状态和分数存储到置换表中 self.transposition_table[board_hash] = (best_score, depth) # 使用LRU缓存 if len(self.transposition_table) > self.max_cache_size: self.transposition_table.popitem(last=False) return best_score def get_valid_moves(self): """获取有效的落子位置，优先考虑已经有棋子的周围，并根据距离排序""" moves = [] for row in range(self.board_size): for col in range(self.board_size): if self.board[row][col] == 0: # 计算距离中心的距离，并根据距离排序，距离越近，优先级越高 distance = abs(row - self.board_size // 2) + abs(col - self.board_size // 2) moves.append((distance, (row, col))) moves.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [move[1] for move in moves] # 只返回坐标 def has_neighbor(self, row, col): """检查周围是否有棋子""" for i in range(max(0, row - 2), min(self.board_size, row + 3)): for j in range(max(0, col - 2), min(self.board_size, col + 3)): if self.board[i][j] != 0: return True return False def is_terminal(self): """检查是否达到终止状态""" for row in range(self.board_size): for col in range(self.board_size): if self.board[row][col] != 0 and self.check_game_over(row, col): return True return len(self.get_valid_moves()) == 0 def evaluate(self): score = 0 for row in range(self.board_size): for col in range(self.board_size): if self.board[row][col] != 0: score += self.evaluate_point(row, col) return score def evaluate_point(self, row, col): piece = self.board[row][col] score = 0 # 位置权重 center = self.board_size // 2 distance_from_center = max(abs(row - center), abs(col - center)) position_weight = 1 - (distance_from_center / center) score += position_weight * 10 # 检查四个方向 directions = [(1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (1, -1)] for dr, dc in directions: line = self.get_line(row, col, (dr, dc)) score += self.evaluate_line(line, piece) return score if piece == 2 else -score def evaluate_line(self, line, piece): score = 0 opponent = 3 - piece # 连五 if [piece] * 5 in [line[i:i+5] for i in range(5)]: score += 1000000 # 活四 if [0, piece, piece, piece, piece, 0] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)]: score += 50000 # 冲四 if [opponent, piece, piece, piece, piece, 0] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)] or \ [0, piece, piece, piece, piece, opponent] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)]: score += 10000 # 活三 if [0, piece, piece, piece, 0] in [line[i:i+5] for i in range(5)]: score += 5000 # 眠三 if [opponent, piece, piece, piece, 0, 0] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)] or \ [0, 0, piece, piece, piece, opponent] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)]: score += 1000 # 活二 if [0, 0, piece, piece, 0, 0] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)]: score += 500 # 眠二 if [opponent, 0, piece, piece, 0, 0] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)] or \ [0, 0, piece, piece, 0, opponent] in [line[i:i+6] for i in range(4)]: score += 100 return score def get_line(self, row, col, direction): """获取指定方向的线""" line = [] for i in range(-5, 6): # 扩展范围以检测更多棋型 r = row + i * direction[0] c = col + i * direction[1] if 0 <= r < self.board_size and 0 <= c < self.board_size: line.append(self.board[r][c]) else: line.append(-1) # 超出边界用 -1 表示 return line def hash_board(self): """将棋盘状态转换为哈希值""" return hash(str(self.board)) def on_closing(self): """处理窗口关闭事件""" print(f"退出线程。") # 调试信息 self.exiting = True # 设置退出标志位 # 等待 AI 计算线程结束 if hasattr(self, 'computer_thread') and self.computer_thread.is_alive(): self.computer_thread.join() self.window.destroy() # 启动游戏 if __name__ == "__main__": game = Gomoku() game.window.mainloop() ```
